new_statements.quote: [p. 82] Polysyllabic phonological words in Tawrã are the locus of interaction between tone and stress; word-level pitch features are determined, or rather, are isomorphic with the abstract metrical structure of stress. ... the overall stress system can be defined thus: Stress falls of the first heavy syllable from left to right. The weight of a syllable is lexically determined and does not change. Stress on the initial syllable (trochaic pattern) will define a syllable as heavy. [p. 84] Tawrã falls into the second group of languages where stress is unpredictable (free stress languages) as evidenced by a number of stressed-based minimal pairs. ... As a general tendency, iambic words are much more common than trochaic words in the language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has exactly one stressed syllable, which is also the sole tone-bearing syllable (four tones). In disyllables stress is either on the second syllable (iambic, the common case; all four tones possible) or on the first (trochaic; only high-falling tone). Hotz formalises this as 'stress on the first heavy syllable', but syllable weight is lexically assigned and not recoverable from the surface in trochaic words, so placement is lexically contrastive (segmental minimal pairs such as ˈkhünyüm 'supernatural being' vs khüˈnyüm 'rattle'); phonetic cues of stress cannot be separated from those of tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described: a phonological word has 'minimally and maximally one heavy syllable, which attracts both stress and tone' (p. 62/67); unstressed light syllables are toneless (default mid pitch) and subject to reduction.
new_statements.exceptions: Trochaic words neutralise tone (HF-M only); clitics/grammatical words carry no main stress (fn. 10 p. 83); native trisyllabic morphemes are rare and have only three tonal patterns (sec. 2.5.6, after Evans & Manyu 2021); unstressed presyllables may lose onset or nucleus (kalà > klà).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root plus affixes; one stress/tone per word); analysis based on citation forms and connected speech from Lohit-district (India) speakers; Chinese-side Darang sources instead transcribe a tone on every syllable (Hotz p. 40; Namkung 1996 pp. 88-89).
new_statements.identity_note: dara1255 is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 CR 2007-021 retired [dat] Darang Deng and merged it into [mhu] Digaro Mishmi (Glottolog diga1241 'Tawra'), 'Darang' being the Chinese-side name (Zayü/Chayu County, Tibet) for the same language. The quoted statement (Hotz 2025) describes Tawrã as spoken in Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh, India. The only material seen for the Chinese-side Darang variety proper is second-hand (Namkung 1996 pp. 88-89 < Sun et al. 1980, 1991: Xiani village, Chayu), which gives four syllable tones and a neutralised first syllable in disyllables but no stress statement; Hotz (p. 40) notes the Chinese sources mark tone on every syllable, unlike his word-level tone/stress analysis. A catalog entry should be filed under diga1241, with dara1255 as an alias.

tone_statements.citation: Evans, Jonathan P. & Johakso Manyu. 2021. The sounds of Tawrã (Digaru-Mishmi), a Tibeto-Burman language. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 44(1): 1-26.
tone_statements.quote: Jiang et al. (2013) identifies High, High-Falling, Mid-Rising, and Mid-Falling tones. Blench (n.d.) lists High, Low, Rising, and Falling tones. Neither of these two publications proposes a neutral, toneless specification. [...] The forms in Jiang et al. (2013; e.g., 33–34) do not exactly match what is found in the dialects of Arunachal Pradesh; e.g., their form /hɑ55 lo55/ corresponds, but is not identical to, to our mid-toned /hɑ lo/ ‘moon’. Because tonal oppositions are not presented in minimal pairs in Jiang et al. (2013), it is not yet clear if the difference recorded between Chinese and Indian dialects is due to dialectal variation, or some other reason.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.6 pp. 82-86: one stress (= one tone) per phonological word; 'Stress falls of the first heavy syllable from left to right. The weight of a syllable is lexically determined'; disyllables are trochaic (HF-M only) or iambic (M + any of 4 tones); p. 84 'Tawrã falls into the second group of languages where stress is unpredictable (free stress languages)' with segmental minimal pairs (Table 2.22); iambic far more common; stress cues cannot be separated from tone.
